name: Carla Alvarez

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for meeting me, Carla. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to AI companies, employers, unions or government, and what you tell me stays confidential. What's a normal working day for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I drive an eight-wheel tipper for the quarry up on the hill road. I get weighed on the weighbridge, that's the big scale at the gate, load up with gravel or sand, and run it to building sites, farms and the odd garden job. Six or seven loads on a good day. I like the bit where you tip on a slope and get it exactly where the groundworker wants it without getting bogged in.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I rent a little terrace on Quarry Lane, which is funny, with my dog Biscuit. I'm on my own, so it's all on my wage, and I've got maybe three weeks of bills put by. I don't use AI stuff and I don't really want to. My phone's for calls and the football scores.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. I'll read it as written. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fair enough, I never believed it anyway. I don't post online, so I'd just say it in the weighbridge office over a brew. Most of the drivers would agree with me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It doesn't change my real problem, which is winter. From December to February the quarry goes quiet and they cut us to three days. I get through that every year by running my savings to zero. AI being hype doesn't help with that at all.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing what I'm doing. I'd try to save a bit more in summer when there's overtime, so winter isn't so tight. Maybe ask about covering the loading shovel in winter, if they'd let me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as now, which is a bit worried. Not panicking, just counting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does a bad winter look like for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two winters ago I had a hundred left in the bank by February and Biscuit, my dog, needed the vet. I put it on a credit card and I'm still paying it off. That's what keeps me awake, not robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said maybe the loading shovel. What would that take?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A ticket, a short course on the shovel. The quarry would have to pay for it, because I can't. The manager's fair, so I'd ask, but I wouldn't hold my breath.

say: I'd say I **never believed** the hype anyway.
I'd say it over a brew in the **weighbridge office**, not online.
think: My real problem is **winter**, when the quarry cuts us to three days.
I run my savings to **zero** every winter, and hype doesn't change that.
do: Save **summer overtime** to cover the winter short weeks.
Ask about a **loading shovel** ticket for winter cover.
feel: **Worried** in the same way as now, **counting** rather than panicking.
S0.quote: Two winters ago I had a hundred left in the bank by February and Biscuit, my dog, needed the vet.
fieldNote: Carla's anxiety comes from **seasonal short weeks** at the quarry, not technology.
A **credit card** debt from a vet bill still hangs over her.
She's practical and **low-expectation** about asking her employer for help.

steps.text: Save summer overtime to cover three-day winter weeks
Ask the quarry manager to fund a loading shovel ticket
Keep running gravel and sand loads in the tipper

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's the office that needs to worry. Somebody's still got to back a tipper onto a muddy site and not roll it. I'd say it to anyone who asked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Thinking about it, the weighbridge and the bookings are already half computer. If AI takes the rest, the quarry might let the booking girl go, and then the loads get planned tighter. Tighter plans mean they could manage with one less tipper. There aren't many quarries round here to go to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my head down and do the job well, so I'm not the one they let go. I'd stop the gym membership, which I barely use. And if they make us use some new app, I'd learn it, grumbling.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, and a bit annoyed. I don't like things changing for no reason I can see.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at the quarry would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sandra, who does the bookings and the tickets. She's been there longer than me and she's a single mum. If AI is answering customers and booking loads, Sandra on bookings is the first one gone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you speak up for her?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say something to the manager, yeah. I'm not a union type, but you look after the people you work with. That's just being decent.

say: I'd say the **office** should worry, not the drivers.
I'd point out someone still has to back a **tipper** onto a muddy site.
think: The **weighbridge and bookings** go fully to computers first.
Tighter planning could mean **one less tipper**, with few quarries nearby.
do: Work carefully so she isn't the **driver let go**.
Cancel the **gym membership** she barely uses.
Learn any **new app** the quarry brings in, reluctantly.
feel: **Uneasy** and **annoyed** at change she can't see the reason for.
S1.quote: If AI is answering customers and booking loads, Sandra on bookings is the first one gone.
fieldNote: Carla spots that the **booking side** of the quarry changes before the driving.
She worries most for **Sandra**, a colleague with more to lose.
She isn't a union person but believes in **looking after** coworkers.

steps.text: Cancel the gym membership to build a small buffer
Learn whatever load-booking app the quarry brings in
Keep the tipper runs tidy so she isn't the one cut

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say somebody in government had better have a plan, because I don't. I'm not one for marches, but I'd vote for whoever promised to look after workers. That'd be my line.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the quarry would be one of the first places to go driverless, because it's private land and the same routes all day. The big mines already use self-driving dump trucks. Road runs to sites might last till 2031, but I'd be waiting for the letter the whole time. I've got nothing to fall back on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep driving every shift they'd give me and save anything I could. I'd ask my brother in the next town if I could move in with him if it came to it. Beyond that, I honestly don't know what I'd retrain as.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared. I'd be checking the post every morning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with Biscuit if you had to move in with your brother?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's the first thing I thought of, honestly. My brother's got a cat and his girlfriend doesn't like dogs. I'd have to find a way, because Biscuit's all I've got.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the planning goes in 2028 and the driving around 2031. What happens in between?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In between, I'd be driving to a plan made by a machine, with fewer people in the office and everyone nervous. Three years of knowing you're next. I'd rather know the date.

say: I'd say the **government** had better have a plan.
I'd **vote** for whoever promised to look after workers.
think: Quarries go **driverless** early because it's private land and fixed routes.
Road runs might last till **2031**, but I'd have **nothing** to fall back on.
do: Take every **shift** offered and save what she can.
Ask her **brother** if she could move in with him.
feel: **Scared**, checking the post every morning for the letter.
S2.quote: The big mines already use self-driving dump trucks. Road runs to sites might last till 2031, but I'd be waiting for the letter the whole time.
fieldNote: Carla knows **mining trucks** are already driverless, which makes this feel real.
She has **no retraining idea** and says so honestly.
Her dog **Biscuit** is her first concern in any housing change.

steps.text: Take every tipper shift on offer and save the extra
Ask her brother about moving into his house if laid off
Vote for candidates promising protection for displaced workers

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to get people sorted if someone actually bothers. I'd tell the manager we want to know early. No surprises, that's all I'd ask.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Till about 2034, maybe less at the quarry itself. I'd be thirty-four. That's young, but I don't know what I'd do instead, and there's not much round here. I'd probably end up driving something else that's also going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd save harder, maybe a small amount each week into an account I can't touch. I'd look at what the job centre offers for training, which I've never done. And I'd think about whether I'd have to leave the area.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but I could plan a bit. Five years is long enough to sort out a move.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where would you move?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably to the city where my brother is, even though I hate cities. More jobs, more kinds of work. I'd have to find a place that takes dogs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What kind of training would you even look at?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Something with my hands still. Maybe groundworks, driving a digger on sites, though I suppose diggers go robot too. I'd want someone to tell me what's actually safe, because I don't know.

say: I'd say five years is enough if someone **bothers** to plan.
I'd ask the manager for **early warning** and no surprises.
think: The quarry job lasts to about **2034**, maybe less.
I'd probably end up driving something **else that's going** too.
do: Save a little each week into a **locked account**.
Check **job centre training** for the first time.
Consider **moving** to the city where her brother lives.
feel: **Worried** but able to plan a bit, especially a **move**.
S3.quote: I'd want someone to tell me what's actually safe, because I don't know.
fieldNote: Carla's main lever with more time is **moving away**, not retraining.
She wants someone she trusts to say which jobs are **safe**.
Every retraining idea she has is **hands-on**, and she sees robots reaching those too.

steps.text: Put a small sum each week into a locked savings account
Ask the job centre what training courses exist for drivers
Look at renting near her brother in the city

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty, nobody's got an excuse. I'd say it at work and leave it at that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years for the thinking stuff and around 2039 for the trucks. I'd be thirty-nine. That's a long time, and honestly I'd probably just keep going and hope I'm wrong. I'm not proud of that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Year one, I'd change nothing. I'd keep driving and keep saving summer overtime like now. Maybe in five years I'd start looking properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit worried, but it feels a long way off. Like a bill that's due next year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you're not proud of just keeping going. Why?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I know I should plan. But I've never been good at change, and when it's ten years away it's easy to tell yourself next year. I'd probably still be saying that in 2035.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would push you to start sooner?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If they put a self-driving tipper in at the quarry, even on a trial. Seeing it would make it real. Until then, it's just talk.

say: I'd say **ten years** leaves nobody an excuse.
I'd say it at work and **leave it** at that.
think: The trucks go around **2039**, when I'd be thirty-nine.
I'd probably **keep going** and hope I'm wrong, and I'm not proud of it.
do: Change **nothing** in year one and keep driving the quarry tipper.
Keep saving **summer overtime** for winter, as she does now.
Start looking at **other work** properly in about five years.
feel: A bit **worried**, but it feels like a bill due next year.
S4.quote: When it's ten years away it's easy to tell yourself next year. I'd probably still be saying that in 2035.
fieldNote: Carla is honest that a long runway makes her **put things off**.
Only seeing a **self-driving tipper** at the quarry would get her moving.
Her **winter money worries** remain, so she's still anxious underneath.

steps.text: Keep running the quarry tipper with no changes
Keep banking summer overtime for winter short weeks

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. What would help is somebody straight-talking telling me which jobs are safe, and paying for the course. And honestly, help with rent while I switch, because three weeks of savings is nothing.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about people on their own. Everyone talks about families, but if it's just me and the dog, there's no second wage. One job going means everything going.

headlineQuote: If it's just me and the dog, there's no second wage. One job going means everything going.
portrait: Carla is a **27-year-old** quarry tipper driver who lives alone with her dog Biscuit.
She has about **three weeks** of savings and struggles every winter when hours drop.
She's **practical** and avoids AI, judging things case by case rather than by politics.
Fast AGI scares her because quarries are easy to **automate** and she has no plan.
Longer timelines lead her to **put off** planning, which she admits.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because she'd have nothing to fall back on.
whatWouldHelp: Honest advice on **safe jobs**, paid courses and **rent help** during the switch.
